screens.title: Why performance is critical in XR
screens.narratorSegment: Let's define the central claim: XR performance is not optional because human perception and device limits make poor performance harmful. A frame rate that dips below the target for a headset causes latency between head motion and rendered frames. That latency shows as judder or smeared movement and can lead to motion sickness in VR or tracking instability in AR. For example, many headsets expect stable rendering at 72, 80, or 90 frames per second; dropping below those ranges often produces a noticeable difference to users. Beyond frame rate, consistent frame time is important: large spikes are often worse than a small steady drop because spikes break the user's sense of continuity. A common misconception is to optimize visually first—reducing fidelity before understanding if rendering is the bottleneck. Instead, measure with the Profiler to see whether C P U, G P U, or script allocations are the root cause. If you find the C P U is busy issuing hundreds of draw calls, batching might help; if the G P U is bound, reduce pixel cost or texture sizes. Takeaway: always measure, then apply the least invasive fix that addresses the real bottleneck. How might you change a scene to reduce spikes without sacrificing important visual cues?

keyIdea.title: Why it matters
keyIdea.text: High, stable frame rates preserve user comfort and tracking fidelity; spikes and low rates break immersion and can cause sickness.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Why performance is critical in XR
Definition
Performance in XR is the combination of frame rate, frame-time consistency, and low latency between input and rendered output. All three affect user comfort and the accuracy of tracking.
Concrete Example
A VR scene targeting 90 FPS that briefly drops to 45 FPS produces a large frame-time spike that users perceive as stutter. That stutter can cause disorientation and break immersion.
Common Misconception
Randomly lowering texture resolution without profiling can waste time. Always profile to see whether CPU draw calls, GPU shaders, or scripts are the primary cost.
Key Takeaway

Protect frame rate and frame-time stability first; use profiling to choose the correct optimization path.

Why users notice spikes
  • Human vestibular system expects smooth updates; spikes create sensory mismatch.
  • AR tracking can lose alignment when rendering lags, causing jitter in overlays.
  • Small, consistent compromises are sometimes better than large intermittent drops.
What to monitor
  • Frame rate target for the device (platform-specific).
  • Frame-time spikes in the Profiler showing main thread or GPU stalls.
  • SetPass Calls and Batches as indicators of draw call cost.

screens.title: CPU vs GPU bottlenecks
screens.narratorSegment: When performance problems appear, deciding whether the C P U or G P U is the limiter is a crucial step. The C P U prepares draw calls, runs game logic, and schedules work, whereas the G P U renders geometry, executes shaders, and writes pixels. A practical test is to watch the Profiler: if the Main Thread shows long spikes and the Rendering section reports many Batches and SetPass Calls, the C P U overhead of issuing draw calls or heavy scripting is likely the cause. If G P U timings dominate and the G P U frame time is high, then pixel cost, shader complexity, or large textures are the culprits. An example: a dense scene with thousands of individually rendered static props often shows high Batches in Rendering—this points to draw call overhead and benefits from batching. Conversely, a scene with few batches but very long G P U times suggests heavy post-processing or expensive fragment shaders; lowering resolution or simplifying shaders helps. A common misconception is to assume textures are always the problem; textures matter, but only if the G P U shows high memory bandwidth or long fragment times. Close with this rule: profile, identify whether Main Thread or G P U time is the largest contributor, pick the matching class of fixes, and re-profile to verify. What did the Profiler show in your last test scene and which side did it implicate?

keyIdea.title: Diagnosis Rule
keyIdea.text: Use the Profiler to check whether Main Thread or GPU time dominates; pick CPU fixes for Main Thread issues and GPU fixes for GPU-bound frames.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › CPU vs GPU bottlenecks
CPU-bound symptoms
  • High Main Thread time in the Profiler.
  • Large numbers of Batches or SetPass Calls in Rendering.
  • Spikes tied to instantiation, garbage collection, or complex scripting in Update.
Common fixes
  • Static batching, dynamic batching where appropriate.
  • Object pooling to avoid frequent allocations.
  • Cache component references and reduce per-frame allocations.
GPU-bound symptoms
  • High GPU frame time reported by the Profiler.
  • Low number of batches but long fragment or vertex shader times.
  • Performance improves when reducing render resolution.
Common fixes
  • Reduce texture sizes and change compression.
  • Simplify shaders or reduce post-processing effects.
  • Use LODs and reduce overdraw in transparent surfaces.
Quick diagnostic flow
Profile → Is Main Thread or GPU time higher? → Apply corresponding fixes → Re-profile to verify impact.

screens.title: Draw calls and why they matter
screens.narratorSegment: A draw call is the C P U instruction that tells the G P U to render a set of triangles with a specific material and state. Each draw call carries overhead on the C P U: state setup, sending data, and issuing work to the G P U. In Unity, the Profiler shows Batches and SetPass Calls as rough measures of draw call cost. High numbers of small draw calls increase Main Thread time because the C P U spends time preparing and submitting many separate requests. For example, a forest rendered as many independent tree objects each with the same material can produce hundreds of draw calls; marking those trees as Static and enabling static batching lets Unity combine them into a single large mesh at build time, drastically reducing the number of draw calls. A common misconception is that dynamic batching will handle everything automatically; dynamic batching only applies to small meshes with certain restrictions and does not replace static batching for large static scenes. Key practice: group objects that share materials, prefer shared materials where appropriate, and use batching when objects are non-moving. After batching, re-run the Profiler to confirm that Batches and SetPass Calls drop and Main Thread time improves.

keyIdea.text: Fewer draw calls reduce CPU overhead; static batching is the best fit for many identical, non-moving objects that share a material.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Draw calls and why they matter
What is a draw call?
A draw call is the CPU command to render a set of triangles with a given material and GPU state. Many small draw calls can consume significant CPU time.
Indicators in Unity
  • Profiler: high Batches and SetPass Calls.
  • Scene with many unique objects using separate materials.
Key Takeaway

Reducing draw calls is often the fastest way to lower CPU time for rendering-heavy scenes.

Concrete example
A pack of identical static props like rocks or trees, all sharing a material, can be combined using static batching so the GPU receives a single draw call instead of many.
Common mistake
Relying solely on dynamic batching for large scenes. Dynamic batching is limited to small meshes and has constraints around vertex counts and shader usage.
Action
Mark appropriate GameObjects as Static to enable static batching and re-run the Profiler to compare Batches.

screens.title: Static vs Dynamic Batching
screens.narratorSegment: Static batching and dynamic batching both reduce draw calls, but they target different scenarios and have different constraints. Static batching combines multiple non-moving meshes that share the same material into a single mesh at build time. This yields a dramatic reduction in draw calls for static scenes but requires that the objects do not move and that they share materials. Dynamic batching happens at runtime for small meshes and can cover moving objects, but it has limits: it only applies to meshes below certain vertex counts and performance gains can vary. For example, a set of 200 rocks that never move and share a material are ideal for static batching; Unity will combine them into fewer draw calls during the build. Conversely, a character with many animated small props might benefit from dynamic batching but will still be constrained by vertex counts and shader complexity. A frequent misconception is to mark everything static by default: that can increase build time and memory since combined meshes are created. Best practice: mark only truly static geometry as Static, keep shared materials where appropriate, and rely on dynamic batching only for small, moving meshes that meet Unity's constraints. After applying batching, re-profile to confirm that Batches and SetPass Calls drop and that the Main Thread time improves.

Best practice: mark only truly static geometry as Static, keep shared materials where appropriate, and rely on dynamic batching only for small, moving meshes that meet Unity's constraints. After applying batching, re-profile to confirm that Batches and SetPass Calls drop and that the Main Thread time improves.

keyIdea.title: Batching Guidance
keyIdea.text: Use static batching for non-moving, shared-material objects; reserve dynamic batching for small runtime meshes that meet Unity's constraints.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Static vs Dynamic Batching
Static Batching
Combines non-moving meshes that share a material into a single mesh at build time. Best for large numbers of identical props that will not move.
Pros
  • Massive reduction in draw calls for static scenes.
  • Low runtime CPU overhead for rendering those objects.
Cons
  • Increased build time and potentially higher memory for combined meshes.
  • Not suitable for moving objects.
Dynamic Batching
Combines small meshes at runtime to reduce draw calls for moving objects, but only when meshes meet specific size and shader constraints.
Pros
  • Can reduce draw calls for small, moving meshes without marking them static.
Cons
  • Limited by vertex count, material properties, and shader complexity.
  • Not a replacement for static batching on large numbers of static objects.
Practical rule
Mark only truly static geometry as Static for batching; use dynamic batching selectively and always profile the results.

screens.title: Occlusion Culling: Bake and apply
screens.narratorSegment: Occlusion culling prevents rendering objects that are fully hidden behind other geometry from the camera's perspective. Unlike frustum culling, which skips objects outside the camera view, occlusion culling must be baked ahead of runtime so Unity can use visibility data to decide what to draw. The typical workflow is: mark static occluders and occludees in the Inspector, open the Occlusion Culling window under Rendering, configure parameters such as Smallest Occluder and Smallest Hole if needed, and click Bake. Once baked, Unity uses the precomputed visibility set at runtime to avoid sending occluded objects to the G P U, which reduces draw calls and G P U workload in scenes with complex occlusion like interiors. For example, inside a building, walls and large furniture act as occluders so many distant objects need not be rendered when they lie behind a wall. Beware of a misconception: occlusion culling helps only when many objects are obscured from view; in fully open outdoor scenes with few occluders, baking provides little benefit. Always test by moving the camera while watching Profiler Batches and SetPass Calls and confirm the expected reduction. Finally, tune bake settings to avoid overly small occluder thresholds that miss useful culling or overly aggressive settings that cull visible items.

keyIdea.title: Occlusion Culling
keyIdea.text: Bake visibility data for static scenes so Unity can avoid rendering objects hidden behind occluders, reducing GPU work where it matters most.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Occlusion Culling
Bake workflow
  1. Mark large static geometry as "Occluder Static" and potential hidden objects as "Occludee Static".
  2. Open Window → Rendering → Occlusion Culling and review bake settings.
  3. Adjust Smallest Occluder and Smallest Hole if needed, then click Bake to precompute visibility data.
  4. Play and move the camera; verify objects are not rendered when fully occluded and check Profiler counts.
When it helps
Indoor or cluttered scenes with many objects that can be blocked by walls or large props benefit most from baked occlusion culling.
Example Scenario
A museum interior with many exhibits: walls and large display cases occlude distant objects, so baking visibility reduces GPU work as the viewer moves through rooms.
Misconception
Occlusion culling is not a cure-all for open outdoor scenes; it gives most value in environments with clear occluders.
Action
Mark occluders and occludees, bake, then verify Batches drop when objects become hidden during camera movement.

screens.title: Texture optimization and compression
screens.narratorSegment: Textures are a major consumer of G P U memory and bandwidth. Using unnecessarily large textures increases memory footprint and can lengthen G P U frame time, especially on mobile and standalone XR devices with limited resources. The practical rule is to use the smallest texture resolution that still looks good at the size it appears onscreen. For distant or small objects, downscale textures; for large, high-detail surfaces, keep higher resolutions. Use texture compression formats suited to the target platform—mobile platforms often favor ASTC, while desktop GPUs commonly use DXT formats. Compression reduces memory and bandwidth use, but different formats have different visual trade-offs. A common mistake is to compress blindly with defaults; always inspect compressed results on the target device because artifacts can be more visible in some texture types. Also remove unused texture channels and mipmaps where appropriate. Example: a 4K texture used for a small prop is wasteful; replacing it with a 512 or 1024 texture and enabling compression may preserve perceived quality while dramatically reducing memory. After changes, profile G P U memory usage and frame timings to confirm improvements.

keyIdea.title: Texture Rule
keyIdea.text: Match texture resolution and compression to screen size and device capabilities; test compressed results on the target device.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Texture optimization
Practical guidance
  • Use the smallest resolution that looks acceptable at the object's screen size.
  • Enable texture compression appropriate to the target device.
  • Remove unused channels and consider disabling mipmaps for UI atlases where not needed.
Examples
Replace a 4K prop texture with 512 or 1024 where the prop appears small in frame; choose ASTC for many mobile XR targets to balance quality and compression.
Common mistake
Assuming a single compression format works for all devices. Compression artifacts differ by format; always check results on your target hardware.
What to profile
  • GPU memory usage after texture changes.
  • Frame time improvements when reducing texture size or resolution scale.

screens.title: Mesh optimization and LODs
screens.narratorSegment: Meshes contribute to both G P U and C P U cost: they determine how much geometry the G P U must process and how much vertex data the C P U must upload. Optimization strategies include reducing polygon count to the minimum that preserves silhouette and visual fidelity, removing unnecessary vertex data such as tangents or secondary UVs when shaders do not use them, and generating Level of Detail models that switch to cheaper meshes at distance. For instance, a complex prop that is very small on-screen should use a simplified mesh or billboarding at distance to avoid wasting vertex processing. Unity and external DCC tools provide mesh simplification tools; use them iteratively, checking visual impact. A common misconception is to assume vertex count alone defines cost; shader complexity and overdraw also matter. Combine mesh simplification with appropriate shader and texture choices for best results. Test with the Profiler: look at vertex and triangle counts and G P U timings when swapping LODs to ensure the expected savings occur. LODs are especially useful in XR since objects far from the viewpoint can be drawn with far fewer triangles without affecting perceived quality.

A common misconception is to assume vertex count alone defines cost; shader complexity and overdraw also matter. Combine mesh simplification with appropriate shader and texture choices for best results. Test with the Profiler: look at vertex and triangle counts and G P U timings when swapping LODs to ensure the expected savings occur. LODs are especially useful in XR since objects far from the viewpoint can be drawn with far fewer triangles without affecting perceived quality.

keyIdea.title: Mesh Rule
keyIdea.text: Use the lowest polygon count that maintains visual quality, remove unused mesh channels, and employ LODs for distant objects.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Mesh optimization and LODs
Best practices
  • Reduce polygon count while preserving silhouette.
  • Remove unused vertex attributes like tangents if shaders don't need them.
  • Implement LODs for objects that can be simplified at distance.
When to simplify
If an object's screen size is small or rarely inspected up close, a simplified mesh often suffices and reduces vertex processing cost.
Common mistake
Removing detail where it is visible at close range. Always evaluate LOD switch distances and inspect transitions for popping or quality loss.
Testing tip
Profile scene performance while moving the camera to trigger LOD transitions; confirm triangle counts and GPU time drop as expected.

screens.title: Lighting: baked lightmaps and probes
screens.narratorSegment: Real-time lighting is expensive in XR, particularly when multiple dynamic lights and shadows are involved. Baked lighting converts static lighting and shadow information into textures, called lightmaps, which are cheap to sample at runtime. Use Unity's Lightmapping system to bake static scene lighting for environments that don't require dynamic changes. For dynamic objects that still need to appear consistent with baked lighting, use light probes which capture lighting at sample points and allow dynamic renderers to receive baked illumination approximations. A practical workflow: mark static geometry appropriately, set up your light sources and bake settings, generate lightmaps, and place light probes where dynamic objects move. An example: in a furnished room, bake global illumination for walls and floors; add light probes so a moving character appears lit correctly when walking through the space. Avoid the misconception that baked lighting eliminates the need for any dynamic lighting; dynamic lights are still necessary for moving light sources but should be limited in number and scope. After baking, verify runtime performance and visual fidelity, since lightmaps trade precompute time and disk memory for runtime savings.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Lighting: baked lightmaps
Baked lighting benefits
  • Precomputes expensive global illumination and shadows into textures.
  • Reduces runtime cost significantly for static scenes.
Light probes
Capture baked lighting at sample points so dynamic objects can receive consistent indirect lighting without full dynamic GI.
Workflow
  1. Mark static geometry and set appropriate lightmap UVs.
  2. Choose bake settings and generate lightmaps via Window → Lighting → Settings.
  3. Place light probes to cover regions where dynamic objects move.
  4. Test runtime appearance and performance.
Misconception
Baked lighting is not a replacement for needed dynamic lights; dynamic lights should be limited and tuned for range and intensity to reduce cost.

screens.title: Physics optimization and Fixed Timestep
screens.narratorSegment: Physics calculations can be a hidden C P U cost in XR. Each active Rigidbody and collider contributes to collision detection and resolution steps that run on fixed update intervals. To reduce physics overhead, minimize the number of active Rigidbodies, prefer simple colliders like boxes or spheres instead of expensive mesh colliders, and avoid unnecessary kinematic Rigidbodies that still interact with the physics engine. You can also increase the Fixed Timestep in Project Settings if high-frequency physics updates are unnecessary; for example, moving from a very small timestep to something like 0.02 yields fewer physics updates per second and reduces C P U load when precise simulation is not needed. Use continuous collision detection only where required and disable physics for distant objects. A common error is reducing the timestep without considering gameplay impact; changing timestep affects determinism and simulation fidelity. Example: a scene with many small collectibles can use simple colliders and avoid Rigidbody simulation until the player approaches, or switch to trigger-based activation to limit active physics. Profile C P U Main Thread time before and after changes to ensure the expected savings.

Practical tips
  • Prefer Box, Sphere, and Capsule colliders over Mesh Colliders where possible.
  • Reduce the number of active Rigidbodies and use kinematic where appropriate.
  • Adjust Fixed Timestep in Project Settings to lower physics update frequency if precision allows.
Activation patterns
Delay enabling physics for distant objects or use triggers that only activate simulation when the player is nearby.
Common mistake
Overusing mesh colliders and enabling many rigidbodies unnecessarily. Simplify colliders or combine into fewer physics actors.
Key Takeaway

Tune physics complexity to actual gameplay needs and profile to ensure changes reduce Main Thread time.

screens.title: Profiler-driven workflow and object pooling
screens.narratorSegment: The most reliable optimizations start with the Unity Profiler. Measure C P U and G P U usage, find spikes on the Main Thread or long G P U frames, and look at rendering statistics such as Batches and SetPass Calls. Focus on the largest contributor and avoid changing multiple systems at once. One frequent hotspot in XR is frequent Instantiate and Destroy calls that create allocation spikes and garbage collection. Replace these with object pooling: allocate a fixed pool of objects at Awake, deactivate extras, and reuse them by toggling active state. The code example on the screen shows a simple ObjectPool that pre-instantiates a list of objects, returns inactive ones when requested, and deactivates returned objects. A common misconception is that adding pooling always solves C P U spikes; pooling helps allocation and GC pressure, but if your bottleneck is draw calls or shader cost, pooling won't help. After implementing pooling, re-run the Profiler and look for reduced GC and smoother Main Thread timings. A final tip: combine profiling with platform testing because desktop and mobile XR devices have very different resource constraints. What did your Profiler reveal as the top two costs in your last test run?

keyIdea.title: Profiler + Pooling
keyIdea.text: Profile to find allocation spikes and replace heavy instantiate/destroy patterns with a fixed-size object pool to reduce GC and runtime spikes.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Profiler & Object Pooling
Profiler workflow
  1. Run the Profiler in Play Mode and capture a session.
  2. Identify the largest CPU or GPU time contributors, and note Batches and SetPass Calls.
  3. Fix one class of problem, then re-run the Profiler to verify improvement.
Scripting hotspots
Look for allocation spikes, frequent Instantiate/Destroy calls, and heavy per-frame logic in Update.
Object Pool Example
A simple pool pre-instantiates objects and reuses them instead of destroying and creating new instances at runtime.
// Simple Object Pool Example
public class ObjectPool : MonoBehaviour
{
    public GameObject prefab;
    public int poolSize = 10;
    private List pooledObjects = new List();

    void Awake()
    {
        for (int i = 0; i < poolSize; i++)
        {
            GameObject obj = Instantiate(prefab);
            obj.SetActive(false);
            pooledObjects.Add(obj);
        }
    }

    public GameObject GetPooledObject()
    {
        foreach (GameObject obj in pooledObjects)
        {
            if (!obj.activeInHierarchy)
            {
                return obj;
            }
        }
        GameObject newObj = Instantiate(prefab);
        pooledObjects.Add(newObj);
        return newObj;
    }

    public void ReturnPooledObject(GameObject obj)
    {
        obj.SetActive(false);
    }
}
Check your understanding

After implementing pooling, measure GC and Main Thread spikes; pooling reduces allocation overhead but does not fix draw call or shader-bound issues.

screens.title: Key Concepts — What to Remember
screens.narratorSegment: Here are three compact concepts to remember as you work on XR performance. First, frame rate and frame-time stability are the baseline: aim for the device target and avoid spikes that break comfort. Second, draw calls matter: reduce Batches and SetPass Calls by using static batching for non-moving shared-material objects and by organizing materials sensibly. Third, profile first: use the Unity Profiler to identify whether the C P U or G P U is the bottleneck, then apply targeted fixes like texture compression, mesh simplification, baked lighting, occlusion culling, or object pooling. Keep testing on your target device because desktop and mobile XR hardware behave differently. These three reminders guide most practical optimization workflows: measure, target the largest cost, apply the least invasive fix, and verify results. fullNarratorScript:
In XR, performance is more than speed: it underpins comfort, tracking fidelity, and the user's sense of presence. In this lesson you will learn why consistent frame rates matter, common places where Unity projects stall, and specific techniques you can apply to reduce rendering and C P U overhead. We'll focus on draw call reduction, batching, occlusion culling, optimizing textures and meshes, baking lighting, improving physics performance, scripting patterns such as object pooling, and using the Unity Profiler as an evidence-driven workflow. For example, if a VR scene drops well below the platform target frame rate, users can quickly feel nausea or loss of presence; resolving that often begins by identifying whether the C P U or G P U is the bottleneck. You will also gain a practical hands-on sequence: measure with the Profiler, apply a targeted fix such as static batching or occlusion culling, then measure again to confirm improvement. Throughout, we will call out common misconceptions—like randomly downscaling textures before profiling—and give guidelines for platform-specific choices. By the end of this chapter you will be able to find the largest bottleneck, apply the right optimization pattern, and verify that your changes actually improve runtime performance.

Over the next screens you will develop practical skills for diagnosing and reducing performance problems in Unity XR projects. First, you will understand why high, consistent frame rates are necessary for user comfort in VR and reliable tracking in AR, with concrete frame-rate targets. Second, you will learn to identify common performance bottlenecks such as excessive draw calls, heavy shaders, large textures, and physics overhead. Third, you will apply targeted techniques: static batching, occlusion culling, appropriate texture compression, mesh simplification, and baked lighting. Finally, you will use the Unity Profiler to find the largest bottleneck, then iterate—profile, fix, profile again. For each objective I will describe a short example and a misconception to avoid, so you can apply these skills on real scenes. Completing these objectives will let you reduce C P U and G P U workload in ways that preserve visual quality while protecting frame rate and immersion.

These practical objectives map directly to everyday XR problems. You will be able to detect whether a frame-rate problem is caused by too many draw calls, heavy pixel shading, or expensive C P U work like physics and garbage collection. For example, you might profile a crowded outdoor scene and see hundreds of batches; marking identical static props as Static and enabling static batching will often collapse many draw calls into one and immediately reduce C P U overhead. You will also learn to bake occlusion culling for complex indoor spaces so hidden geometry never reaches the G P U. For asset optimization, you will pick texture resolutions and compression formats appropriate to the device and remove unused mesh channels. In scripting, you will replace frequent instantiate-destroy patterns with a fixed-size object pool to avoid allocation spikes. Each objective includes a small mnemonic and a verified competency mark so you can test your understanding on the supplied hands-on activity. Keep a profiling loop: measure, change one thing, measure again. That disciplined loop prevents wasted effort on irrelevant optimizations.

Let's define the central claim: XR performance is not optional because human perception and device limits make poor performance harmful. A frame rate that dips below the target for a headset causes latency between head motion and rendered frames. That latency shows as judder or smeared movement and can lead to motion sickness in VR or tracking instability in AR. For example, many headsets expect stable rendering at 72, 80, or 90 frames per second; dropping below those ranges often produces a noticeable difference to users. Beyond frame rate, consistent frame time is important: large spikes are often worse than a small steady drop because spikes break the user's sense of continuity. A common misconception is to optimize visually first—reducing fidelity before understanding if rendering is the bottleneck. Instead, measure with the Profiler to see whether C P U, G P U, or script allocations are the root cause. If you find the C P U is busy issuing hundreds of draw calls, batching might help; if the G P U is bound, reduce pixel cost or texture sizes. Takeaway: always measure, then apply the least invasive fix that addresses the real bottleneck. How might you change a scene to reduce spikes without sacrificing important visual cues?

When performance problems appear, deciding whether the C P U or G P U is the limiter is a crucial step. The C P U prepares draw calls, runs game logic, and schedules work, whereas the G P U renders geometry, executes shaders, and writes pixels. A practical test is to watch the Profiler: if the Main Thread shows long spikes and the Rendering section reports many Batches and SetPass Calls, the C P U overhead of issuing draw calls or heavy scripting is likely the cause. If G P U timings dominate and the G P U frame time is high, then pixel cost, shader complexity, or large textures are the culprits. An example: a dense scene with thousands of individually rendered static props often shows high Batches in Rendering—this points to draw call overhead and benefits from batching. Conversely, a scene with few batches but very long G P U times suggests heavy post-processing or expensive fragment shaders; lowering resolution or simplifying shaders helps. A common misconception is to assume textures are always the problem; textures matter, but only if the G P U shows high memory bandwidth or long fragment times. Close with this rule: profile, identify whether Main Thread or G P U time is the largest contributor, pick the matching class of fixes, and re-profile to verify. What did the Profiler show in your last test scene and which side did it implicate?

A draw call is the C P U instruction that tells the G P U to render a set of triangles with a specific material and state. Each draw call carries overhead on the C P U: state setup, sending data, and issuing work to the G P U. In Unity, the Profiler shows Batches and SetPass Calls as rough measures of draw call cost. High numbers of small draw calls increase Main Thread time because the C P U spends time preparing and submitting many separate requests. For example, a forest rendered as many independent tree objects each with the same material can produce hundreds of draw calls; marking those trees as Static and enabling static batching lets Unity combine them into a single large mesh at build time, drastically reducing the number of draw calls. A common misconception is that dynamic batching will handle everything automatically; dynamic batching only applies to small meshes with certain restrictions and does not replace static batching for large static scenes. Key practice: group objects that share materials, prefer shared materials where appropriate, and use batching when objects are non-moving. After batching, re-run the Profiler to confirm that Batches and SetPass Calls drop and Main Thread time improves.

Static batching and dynamic batching both reduce draw calls, but they target different scenarios and have different constraints. Static batching combines multiple non-moving meshes that share the same material into a single mesh at build time. This yields a dramatic reduction in draw calls for static scenes but requires that the objects do not move and that they share materials. Dynamic batching happens at runtime for small meshes and can cover moving objects, but it has limits: it only applies to meshes below certain vertex counts and performance gains can vary. For example, a set of 200 rocks that never move and share a material are ideal for static batching; Unity will combine them into fewer draw calls during the build. Conversely, a character with many animated small props might benefit from dynamic batching but will still be constrained by vertex counts and shader complexity. A frequent misconception is to mark everything static by default: that can increase build time and memory since combined meshes are created. Best practice: mark only truly static geometry as Static, keep shared materials where appropriate, and rely on dynamic batching only for small, moving meshes that meet Unity's constraints. After applying batching, re-profile to confirm that Batches and SetPass Calls drop and that the Main Thread time improves.

Occlusion culling prevents rendering objects that are fully hidden behind other geometry from the camera's perspective. Unlike frustum culling, which skips objects outside the camera view, occlusion culling must be baked ahead of runtime so Unity can use visibility data to decide what to draw. The typical workflow is: mark static occluders and occludees in the Inspector, open the Occlusion Culling window under Rendering, configure parameters such as Smallest Occluder and Smallest Hole if needed, and click Bake. Once baked, Unity uses the precomputed visibility set at runtime to avoid sending occluded objects to the G P U, which reduces draw calls and G P U workload in scenes with complex occlusion like interiors. For example, inside a building, walls and large furniture act as occluders so many distant objects need not be rendered when they lie behind a wall. Beware of a misconception: occlusion culling helps only when many objects are obscured from view; in fully open outdoor scenes with few occluders, baking provides little benefit. Always test by moving the camera while watching Profiler Batches and SetPass Calls and confirm the expected reduction. Finally, tune bake settings to avoid overly small occluder thresholds that miss useful culling or overly aggressive settings that cull visible items.

Textures are a major consumer of G P U memory and bandwidth. Using unnecessarily large textures increases memory footprint and can lengthen G P U frame time, especially on mobile and standalone XR devices with limited resources. The practical rule is to use the smallest texture resolution that still looks good at the size it appears onscreen. For distant or small objects, downscale textures; for large, high-detail surfaces, keep higher resolutions. Use texture compression formats suited to the target platform—mobile platforms often favor ASTC, while desktop GPUs commonly use DXT formats. Compression reduces memory and bandwidth use, but different formats have different visual trade-offs. A common mistake is to compress blindly with defaults; always inspect compressed results on the target device because artifacts can be more visible in some texture types. Also remove unused texture channels and mipmaps where appropriate. Example: a 4K texture used for a small prop is wasteful; replacing it with a 512 or 1024 texture and enabling compression may preserve perceived quality while dramatically reducing memory. After changes, profile G P U memory usage and frame timings to confirm improvements.

Meshes contribute to both G P U and C P U cost: they determine how much geometry the G P U must process and how much vertex data the C P U must upload. Optimization strategies include reducing polygon count to the minimum that preserves silhouette and visual fidelity, removing unnecessary vertex data such as tangents or secondary UVs when shaders do not use them, and generating Level of Detail models that switch to cheaper meshes at distance. For instance, a complex prop that is very small on-screen should use a simplified mesh or billboarding at distance to avoid wasting vertex processing. Unity and external DCC tools provide mesh simplification tools; use them iteratively, checking visual impact. Combine mesh simplification with appropriate shader and texture choices for best results. Test with the Profiler: look at vertex and triangle counts and G P U timings when swapping LODs to ensure the expected savings occur. LODs are especially useful in XR since objects far from the viewpoint can be drawn with far fewer triangles without affecting perceived quality.

Real-time lighting is expensive in XR, particularly when multiple dynamic lights and shadows are involved. Baked lighting converts static lighting and shadow information into textures, called lightmaps, which are cheap to sample at runtime. Use Unity's Lightmapping system to bake static scene lighting for environments that don't require dynamic changes. For dynamic objects that still need to appear consistent with baked lighting, use light probes which capture lighting at sample points and allow dynamic renderers to receive baked illumination approximations. A practical workflow: mark static geometry appropriately, set up your light sources and bake settings, generate lightmaps, and place light probes where dynamic objects move. An example: in a furnished room, bake global illumination for walls and floors; add light probes so a moving character appears lit correctly when walking through the space. Avoid the misconception that baked lighting eliminates the need for any dynamic lighting; dynamic lights are still necessary for moving light sources but should be limited in number and scope. After baking, verify runtime performance and visual fidelity, since lightmaps trade precompute time and disk memory for runtime savings.

Physics calculations can be a hidden C P U cost in XR. Each active Rigidbody and collider contributes to collision detection and resolution steps that run on fixed update intervals. To reduce physics overhead, minimize the number of active Rigidbodies, prefer simple colliders like boxes or spheres instead of expensive mesh colliders, and avoid unnecessary kinematic Rigidbodies that still interact with the physics engine. You can also increase the Fixed Timestep in Project Settings if high-frequency physics updates are unnecessary; for example, moving from a very small timestep to something like 0.02 yields fewer physics updates per second and reduces C P U load when precise simulation is not needed. Use continuous collision detection only where required and disable physics for distant objects. A common error is reducing the timestep without considering gameplay impact; changing timestep affects determinism and simulation fidelity. Example: a scene with many small collectibles can use simple colliders and avoid Rigidbody simulation until the player approaches, or switch to trigger-based activation to limit active physics. Profile C P U Main Thread time before and after changes to ensure the expected savings.

Measure C P U and G P U usage, find spikes on the Main Thread or long G P U frames, and look at rendering statistics such as Batches and SetPass Calls. Focus on the largest contributor and avoid changing multiple systems at once. Keep these three quick references at hand when optimizing XR scenes. First, texture and mesh choices: match resolutions and LODs to screen size and device to minimize G P U work. Second, lighting and occlusion: bake lightmaps for static geometry and use occlusion culling to avoid rendering hidden objects. Third, script-level efficiencies: avoid per-frame allocations, cache references, and pool frequently created objects to reduce GC and Main Thread spikes. Use these reminders as a checklist when you run the Profiler: if G P U time is high, inspect textures, shaders, and lighting; if Main Thread time is high, inspect batches, instantiation patterns, and physics.
